title: Buzzards Club Saturday dances and colored bands
summary: They discuss the Buzzards' biweekly dances, the use of Black bands, carnival marches and a diminished carnival.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Joe I'm trying to think of those Saturday night dances. Joe I went to only two or three of them I guess. Joe Ten years ago. Joe Was that at the Buzzards Club every other Saturday wasn't it?

Joe Yeah well the Buzzards had one every other Saturday. Joe In fact the Buzzards used to run every other Saturday when we was playing at Tyler's. Joe You see now we used to get that same crowd the same Buzzard crowd used to follow our band up to Tyler's. Joe Yeah. Joe You see. Joe But the Buzzards they had been running every other Saturday night for at least like you say 10 or 12 years. Joe But it was in the old hall. Joe See now after they built the new home well then they started giving them every Saturday night and they just was using colored bands occasionally. Joe You see they was using white bands well. Joe Last time I went by it sounded like a hillbilly band in there.

Joe Yeah. Joe And then they would use colored bands because a couple of them old timers in that club they liked the Joe. Joe And they used to hire Joe. Joe You know Joe's band and Harold Kristoff he carried a band out there once or twice but the colored bands didn't get very much weight in the new hall with the exception of the carnival marches. Joe Yeah. Joe See now they used to hire every carnival. Joe Now when I was playing with the Eureka band we used to play for the Eleanor's. Joe I played for the Eleanor's with the Eureka band for about I guess for about five or six years. Joe Then at that time Garnier had the buzzers. You hear what I'm talking about? Joe Yeah. Joe Yeah. Joe Well he had the buzzers. Knox and all that bunch they was playing with Garnier. Joe Well then after Garnier gave it up then John took it over and I left the Eureka and went with John. And John held it for about five years. And then the Lions there was behind us every year. They wanted to get us. So finally John left the buzzers and went to the Lions. And he could still be playing for the Lions because last year up until last year the Lions hired him but he told them that he's kind of hard of hearing and he had a heart attack. Joe He was sick last year I remember. Joe Yeah he couldn't play so he turned it over to Anderson. Well Anderson tried to get me to play but I told him the hours had got a little bit too much for me. See they come out seven o'clock in the morning and they parade till five in the evening and I had the ulcerized as a leg. Now I can't do all that work. So I told him no I'd rather not bother with it. So the place he called me up and taught me to play with the Zulus with him. He told me it was a short hour. It was a short hour. Joe Yeah it was really good. I was glad I'd take it because they left the river. I went to the river front for nine o'clock and about quarter to twelve it was all over. That was the best one I had ever played. I figured it would go longer than that you see because their hours was usually from nine to five. But last year with all that segregation mess coming up and people scared to come out and tell them don't come on the street what was going to happen and all of them. They kind of had some bearings on the...
Joe Yeah they decided to cut it short. Well they didn't stop a lot of the other places did they?

Joe It didn't go to Gertrude Dennis. Joe No it didn't look like a carnival you know what I mean? You didn't see nothing. There was just very few people in the street and it was nothing exciting. Joe And I played with Buddy Petit up on the dance line. Cronlott and Canel in the old dance line used to be up there.
